lessons.title: Principles of Reduction
lessons.body: Reduction is the chemical removal of oxygen from a metal compound to get pure metal. In smelting, we heat metal oxides with a reducing agent so the metal can flow out as liquid. For example, iron oxide (Fe2O3) plus carbon monoxide (CO) gives iron (Fe) and carbon dioxide (CO2). The key is that the reducing agent grabs the oxygen, leaving the metal behind. In Africa, traditional iron smelting used charcoal made from local trees like acacia. The charcoal burns to form CO, which reduces the iron ore. You can see this in action: when you heat black iron oxide with charcoal in a clay furnace, after about 2 hours at 1200Â°C, you get a bloom of iron. The reaction is: Fe2O3 + 3CO â 2Fe + 3CO2. To make reduction work, you need three things: a metal oxide (ore), a reducing agent (carbon or hydrogen), and enough heat. The temperature must be high enough to melt the metal but not so high that the reducing agent burns away too fast. In a small-scale furnace, use a ratio of 1 part ore to 2 parts charcoal by weight. Crush the ore to bean size (about 1 cm) so the gas can reach all surfaces. Stir the charge every 20 minutes to expose fresh material. You can test if reduction is happening by looking for a silvery or metallic shine on the ore pieces. If you see no change after 1 hour, add more charcoal and increase air blast. Remember, reduction is the heart of smeltingâwithout it, you just have hot rock.

lessons.title: Reducing Agents: Carbon, Hydrogen, Metals
lessons.body: A reducing agent is any substance that gives up electrons or takes oxygen away from a metal oxide. In African smelting, carbon is king. Charcoal and coke are cheap, easy to make, and work at high temperatures. Carbon reduces metal oxides at around 1000â1200Â°C. For example, zinc oxide (ZnO) plus carbon (C) gives zinc vapour and carbon monoxide: ZnO + C â Zn + CO. But carbon has limitsâit leaves carbon impurities in the metal. Hydrogen is cleaner. You can make hydrogen by passing steam over red-hot charcoal: C + H2O â CO + H2. Hydrogen reduces iron oxide at lower temperatures (800Â°C) and produces only water vapour as waste. In a small workshop, you can use a steel pipe with steam and charcoal to generate hydrogen. But hydrogen is explosive, so work outdoors and keep flames away. Metals like aluminium and magnesium are powerful reducing agents. Aluminium powder mixed with iron oxide and ignited gives molten iron in the thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al â 2Fe + Al2O3. This reaches 2500Â°C and is used for welding rails. In Africa, thermite is handy for repairing metal tools without a forge. For everyday smelting, stick with charcoal. Buy charcoal from local producersâhardwood charcoal gives more heat than softwood. Use a ratio of 3 kg charcoal per 1 kg ore. If you need very pure metal, use hydrogen from a generator or buy a small electrolyser. But for most village smelters, carbon is the practical choice. Always wear leather gloves and eye protection when handling reducing agents, especially aluminium powder.

lessons.title: Oxidation Reactions in Smelting
lessons.body: Oxidation is the opposite of reductionâit adds oxygen to a metal or removes electrons. In smelting, oxidation is both a problem and a tool. The problem: when you heat metal in air, it oxidizes back to oxide. For example, molten copper exposed to air forms copper oxide (CuO) on the surface. That's why you must keep the furnace reducing (rich in CO) or cover the melt with charcoal. The tool: oxidation helps remove unwanted elements. When you blow air through molten iron, silicon, manganese, and carbon oxidize and float as slag. This is called 'blowing' or 'converting' and is used in steelmaking. In a small cupola furnace, you blow air through tuyeres (clay pipes) into the melt. The oxygen reacts with carbon to form CO2, which escapes. After 15 minutes of blowing, carbon drops from 4% to 1%. But oxidation also wastes metal. If you blow too long, iron oxidizes to iron oxide and you lose yield. A good rule: stop blowing when the sparks from the furnace change from white to orange. You can also use oxidation to roast sulfide ores. Roasting in air at 600â800Â°C turns metal sulfides into oxides, releasing sulfur dioxide (SO2). For example, zinc sulfide (ZnS) plus oxygen gives zinc oxide and SO2: 2ZnS + 3O2 â 2ZnO + 2SO2. That SO2 is toxicânever roast indoors. In Africa, many copper ores are sulfides. Roast them in a shallow pit with a chimney, or better, in a rotating drum. After roasting, the oxide is ready for reduction. Always monitor the colour: black sulfide turns red-brown oxide. Use a pyrometer or just watch the smokeâwhite smoke means SO2, so stand upwind.

lessons.title: Roasting and Calcination
lessons.body: Roasting and calcination are heat treatments that prepare ore for reduction. Roasting uses air to convert sulfides to oxides. Calcination uses heat without air (or with limited air) to drive off water and carbon dioxide. For example, limestone (CaCO3) is calcined to quicklime (CaO) at 900Â°C: CaCO3 â CaO + CO2. In smelting, you calcine limestone to make flux, which removes impurities. Roasting is for sulfide ores. If you have copper pyrite (CuFeS2), roast it at 700Â°C in a stream of air. The sulfur burns off as SO2, leaving a mixture of copper and iron oxides. Then you smelt that with charcoal to get copper. In Africa, small-scale miners often roast ore in open heaps, but that pollutes and wastes sulfur. Better: build a simple roasting kiln from a 200-litre drum. Cut holes at the bottom for air, load crushed ore (2â5 cm pieces) on a grate, and light a wood fire underneath. The fire heats the ore to 600â800Â°C. Stir every 30 minutes. After 2 hours, the ore changes from metallic grey to reddish-brown. That's your signal. Calcination is simpler: put ore or limestone in a closed clay pot and heat to 800â900Â°C for 1 hour. You'll see steam and CO2 bubbling out. For bauxite (aluminium ore), calcination at 1000Â°C removes water: Al2O3Â·2H2O â Al2O3 + 2H2O. Always wear a dust mask when handling calcined materialâit's fine and can hurt your lungs. Store roasted or calcined ore in dry bags. If it gets wet, it will rehydrate and you'll have to redo the process. For a small smelter, roast 10 kg of ore at a time in a drum kiln. Use 2 kg of wood or charcoal as fuel. After roasting, let it cool, then crush to 1 cm for smelting.

lessons.title: Matte Formation and Converting
lessons.body: Matte is a mixture of molten metal sulfides, mainly copper and iron sulfides. It forms when you smelt roasted or raw sulfide ore with a reducing agent and a flux. For example, copper sulfide ore (Cu2S) plus iron sulfide (FeS) melts together at 1000â1100Â°C to form a matte that sinks below the slag. The matte contains 40â70% copper. In Africa, historical copper smelters in Zambia and DR Congo produced matte in clay furnaces. To make matte, charge the furnace with 10 kg sulfide ore, 2 kg charcoal, and 1 kg sand (flux). Heat to 1150Â°C. The matte collects at the bottom. Tap it out into a sand mould. It cools to a dark grey, brittle solid. Converting is the next step: you blow air through molten matte to oxidize the iron and sulfur. Iron oxidizes to FeO, which combines with silica flux to form slag. Sulfur oxidizes to SO2 gas. The remaining copper sulfide reacts with oxygen to form blister copper (98% Cu). The reaction: Cu2S + O2 â 2Cu + SO2. In a small converter, use a clay crucible with a steel pipe for air. Heat the matte to 1200Â°C, then blow air for 20â30 minutes. You'll see a blue-green flame (copper) and white smoke (SO2). Stop when the flame turns green and no more sulfur smells. Pour the copper into ingots. Safety: SO2 is deadly. Always work outdoors or with a fume hood. Wear a respirator with acid gas cartridges. For small-scale, you can skip matte and directly reduce oxide ore, but matte is better for complex sulfides. Practice with 1 kg batches first. Use a propane torch or charcoal forge to melt the matte. Expect 30% copper recovery from matte by weight.

lessons.title: Refining Reactions
lessons.body: Refining removes leftover impurities from smelted metal to get a pure product. The main refining reactions are oxidation and electrolysis. For copper, you first do fire refining: melt blister copper (98% Cu) in a furnace and blow air to oxidize remaining sulfur and iron. Then you add a reducing agent like charcoal or green wood to remove oxygen. The reaction: Cu2O + C â 2Cu + CO. This gives 99.5% pure copper. In Africa, traditional copper smiths use this method. For gold, you use cupellation: melt gold with lead and bone ash. Lead oxidizes to litharge (PbO) and absorbs impurities, leaving pure gold. The reaction: 2Pb + O2 â 2PbO. For iron, refining means removing carbon. You melt pig iron (4% C) and blow oxygen to oxidize carbon to CO2. That's how steel is made. In a small forge, you can refine iron by heating it with iron oxide (hammer scale) and hammering. The carbon diffuses out. For aluminium, you need electrolysis: dissolve alumina (Al2O3) in molten cryolite (Na3AlF6) at 950Â°C and pass 100,000 amps. That's not for small-scale. Instead, refine scrap aluminium by melting and adding a flux like NaCl-KCl to remove oxides. For silver, you use nitric acid to dissolve impurities, then precipitate silver with copper. But that's dangerous. For most African smelters, focus on fire refining: melt your metal, add 1% charcoal by weight, stir for 10 minutes, and skim off slag. Then pour into ingots. Test purity by cooling a sample and checking colourâpure copper is salmon pink, pure gold is bright yellow. Always wear gloves and goggles. Refining produces toxic fumes, so work outside.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Reduction and Oxidation Reactions in African Smelting

This practical reference consolidates the core reaction chemistry covered in the module â reduction principles, reducing agents, oxidation, roasting and calcination, matte formation and converting, and refining â into an operator- and manager-facing guide. It is written for African smelter teams working with copperâcobalt, leadâzinc, tin, ferroalloy, and gold circuits, where feed variability, power constraints, and reagent logistics shape daily decisions. Use it as a bench-side and control-room reference, not as a substitute for plant-specific standard operating procedures.

Why Reaction Chemistry Drives Business Outcomes

In African smelting operations, the cost of getting reduction and oxidation chemistry wrong is measured in lost metal recovery, excessive reductant consumption, refractory damage, and off-spec product that fails to attract premium offtake. A copper smelter in Zambia or the DRC processing 1,000 t/day of concentrate with 25% Cu and 2% Co cannot afford a 3% recovery loss â that is roughly 7.5 t of copper equivalent daily. Similarly, a ferrochrome producer in South Africa's Bushveld Complex lives or dies by the carbon-to-ore ratio and the degree of pre-reduction achieved in the furnace. Understanding the thermodynamics and kinetics of each reaction step allows teams to optimise feed blends, reductant addition, fluxing, and tapping schedules â directly improving margins.

Key Reaction Reference Tables

Table 1: Principal Reduction Reactions by Reducing Agent
Reducing Agent Typical Reaction Temperature Range African Application Example
Carbon (coke, char) MO + C â M + CO 1,100â1,500 Â°C Zambian copper slag cleaning; South African ferrochrome (Bushveld)
Carbon monoxide MO + CO â M + COâ 800â1,200 Â°C Indirect reduction in DRC copperâcobalt furnaces
Hydrogen MO + Hâ â M + HâO 600â1,000 Â°C Pilot DRI/ferroalloy pre-reduction studies (SA, Zimbabwe)
Metallic iron (Fe) CoO + Fe â Co + FeO 1,200â1,400 Â°C DRC cobalt recovery from slag; Zambian converter slag treatment
Metallic aluminium 3MO + 2Al â 3M + AlâOâ 1,500â2,000 Â°C Thermite welding of rail and mill components on mine sites
Silicon (FeSi) 2MO + Si â 2M + SiOâ 1,400â1,600 Â°C Ferrovanadium and ferromanganese production (SA)

Sources: M. A. Reuter et al., Treatise on Process Metallurgy, Vol. 2, Elsevier, 2014; J. J. Eksteen and G. A. Bezuidenhout, "The recovery of cobalt from slags," Journal of the Southern African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, 2006.

Table 2: Oxidation, Roasting and Calcination Reactions â Process Windows
Process Reaction Temperature Atmosphere Purpose
Dead roasting MS + 1.5Oâ â MO + SOâ 600â800 Â°C Excess air Sulphur removal before reduction (Zinc, Cu-Pb)
Partial roasting 2MS + 3Oâ â 2MO + 2SOâ (partial) 500â700 Â°C Controlled air Matte smelting feed prep (Cu, Ni)
Calcination CaCOâ â CaO + COâ 900â1,100 Â°C Air / inert Lime flux production for furnace charge
Sulphating roast MS + 2Oâ â MSOâ 550â700 Â°C Excess air, low T Copperâcobalt leach feed preparation
Converting (Cu) CuâS + Oâ â 2Cu + SOâ 1,200â1,300 Â°C Air / Oâ enriched Blister copper production
Fire refining 2Cu + Oâ â 2CuâO; CuâO + C â 2Cu + CO 1,150â1,250 Â°C Oxidising then reducing Anode copper (0.02â0.05% O)

Sources: W. G. Davenport et al., Extractive Metallurgy of Copper, 5th ed., Elsevier, 2011; R. J. Sinclair, The Extractive Metallurgy of Lead, AusIMM Spectrum Series, 2009.

â  SAFETY WARNING â SOâ, CO, AND MOLTEN METAL HAZARDS

Roasting, calcination, and converting reactions generate sulphur dioxide (SOâ) and carbon monoxide (CO) â both are invisible, potentially lethal gases. SOâ exposure above 2 ppm causes respiratory irritation; above 100 ppm it is immediately dangerous to life. CO is odourless and binds haemoglobin ~210 times more readily than oxygen. In African smelters, acid plant upsets, baghouse failures, and furnace tapping fumes are common exposure pathways.

  • Never tap or charge a furnace without confirmed gas monitoring and local exhaust ventilation.
  • Wear SCBA or supplied-air respirators during converter aisle work â filter masks do not protect against CO.
  • Molten matte and slag react violently with water; keep tap holes, launder channels, and moulds dry.
  • Ensure acid plant is online before initiating sulphide roasting â bypassing scrubbing is a permit-to-work violation.
  • Emergency showers, eye-wash stations, and SOâ/CO detectors must be tested at every shift handover.

Practical Control Levers

Operators and metallurgists can influence reaction outcomes through four primary levers. First, temperature: the Ellingham diagram shows that CO becomes a stronger reductant than carbon at higher temperatures, so furnace hot-zone control directly affects reduction efficiency. Second, oxygen potential: in converting, blowing rate and oxygen enrichment determine whether you produce blister copper or revert to matte. Third, reductant ratio: excess carbon in a ferrochrome furnace wastes energy and increases slag volume; too little leaves unreduced chrome in slag. Fourth, flux basicity: the CaO/SiOâ ratio controls slag viscosity and, in turn, reaction kinetics and metal entrainment.

For African operations, power availability often constrains the ability to hold optimum temperature. Load-shedding in South Africa or diesel generator intermittency in the DRC means furnaces may operate at reduced power, shifting reaction equilibria. In these cases, increasing pre-reduction (using CO from the furnace off-gas) or adjusting feed blend to a lower-melting-point mix can preserve recovery despite energy shortfalls. Documenting these adjustments creates a knowledge base for the next shift.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Verify feed assay and mineralogy before setting reductant and flux ratios â sulphide vs oxide feeds behave very differently in reduction and roasting steps.
  2. Check furnace temperature profile against the target window for each reaction stage; confirm thermocouple calibration and hot-face integrity.
  3. Confirm reductant quality and sizing â carbon content, ash, and particle size affect both reactivity and bed permeability.
  4. Monitor off-gas CO/COâ ratio as a real-time indicator of reduction extent and combustion efficiency.
  5. Maintain slag basicity within specification (typically CaO/SiOâ 0.8â1.2 for many base-metal circuits) to protect refractory and ensure clean metalâslag separation.
  6. Test SOâ and CO detectors at shift start; confirm acid plant and scrubbing systems are online before roasting or converting.
  7. Record all deviations from set-point â temperature, feed rate, oxygen enrichment â with time stamps and corrective actions for trend analysis.
  8. Inspect tapping and launder systems for moisture and wear before every tap; water contact with molten matte causes explosive steam reactions.

Further Reading

  • Southern African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (SAIMM) â peer-reviewed papers on African smelting practice, including copperâcobalt and ferroalloy circuits.
  • Mintek (South Africa) â pyrometallurgy research, testwork services, and technical publications on reduction and refining.
  • The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society (TMS) â conference proceedings on smelting, converting, and refining from global operations.
  • International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) â safety guidance on SOâ, CO, and molten material handling.
  • Davenport et al., Extractive Metallurgy of Copper, 5th ed. â standard reference for converting and fire refining chemistry.

This practical reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills â Smelting Fundamentals course. For plant-specific procedures, always defer to your site's approved SOPs and risk assessments.

quiz.q: What is reduction in smelting?
options: A) Adding oxygen to a metal
B) Removing oxygen from a metal compound
quiz.explanation: Reduction removes oxygen from metal oxides to get pure metal.

quiz.q: Which gas is the main reducing agent when charcoal burns in a smelting furnace?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal burns to form carbon monoxide, which reduces metal oxides.

quiz.q: What is the ideal size for crushing ore before reduction?
quiz.explanation: Bean-size ore allows reducing gas to reach all surfaces.

quiz.q: Which reducing agent produces only water vapour as waste?
quiz.explanation: Hydrogen reduces metal oxides and forms water vapour, not CO2.

quiz.q: What is the thermite reaction used for in Africa?
options: A) Smelting iron ore in a furnace
B) Welding rails without a forge
quiz.explanation: Thermite reaches 2500Â°C and is used for welding metal tools.

quiz.q: What is a practical ratio of charcoal to ore for small-scale smelting?
quiz.explanation: Use about 3 kg charcoal per 1 kg ore for enough heat and reducing gas.

quiz.q: What is oxidation in smelting?
options: A) Removing oxygen from a metal
B) Adding oxygen to a metal or removing electrons
C) Melting metal in a vacuum
quiz.explanation: Oxidation adds oxygen or removes electrons, often forming metal oxides.

quiz.q: Why must you keep molten copper covered with charcoal?
options: A) To add carbon to the copper
B) To prevent oxidation back to copper oxide
C) To make it melt faster
quiz.explanation: Charcoal creates a reducing atmosphere that stops copper from oxidizing.

quiz.q: What does blowing air through molten iron do?
options: A) Adds carbon to the iron
B) Oxidizes silicon, manganese, and carbon
quiz.explanation: Blowing air oxidizes impurities, which float as slag.

quiz.q: How can you tell when to stop blowing air in a small cupola?
options: A) When sparks turn from white to orange
B) When the furnace gets quiet
C) When the slag turns black
quiz.explanation: Sparks change from white to orange when carbon is mostly removed.

quiz.q: What gas is released when roasting zinc sulfide?
quiz.explanation: Roasting sulfides produces sulfur dioxide (SO2).

quiz.q: What is the main difference between roasting and calcination?
options: A) Roasting uses air, calcination uses little or no air
B) Roasting uses water, calcination uses acid
C) Roasting is for oxides, calcination for sulfides
D) Roasting is cold, calcination is hot
quiz.explanation: Roasting requires air to oxidize sulfides; calcination drives off water and CO2 without air.

quiz.q: What is the product of calcining limestone?
quiz.explanation: Calcining limestone (CaCO3) at 900Â°C gives quicklime (CaO) and CO2.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a dust mask when handling calcined material?
options: B) Fine dust can hurt your lungs
quiz.explanation: Calcined material is often fine dust that can damage lungs if inhaled.

quiz.q: What is matte in smelting?
options: B) A mixture of molten metal sulfides
quiz.explanation: Matte is a molten mixture of metal sulfides, mainly copper and iron sulfides.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of converting matte?
options: A) To add sulfur to copper
B) To oxidize iron and sulfur, leaving blister copper
C) To reduce copper oxide to copper
D) To make matte from oxide ore
quiz.explanation: Converting blows air through matte to oxidize iron and sulfur, leaving copper.

quiz.q: What colour flame indicates copper in a converter?
quiz.explanation: Copper gives a blue-green flame during converting.

quiz.q: Why is SO2 dangerous during converting?
options: B) It is deadly if inhaled
quiz.explanation: Sulfur dioxide is toxic and can cause severe lung damage.

quiz.q: What is the first step in fire refining copper?
options: A) Add charcoal to reduce oxygen
B) Blow air to oxidize sulfur and iron
quiz.explanation: Fire refining starts by blowing air to oxidize remaining impurities.

quiz.q: What reaction removes oxygen from copper during fire refining?
options: C) CuS + O2 â Cu + SO2
D) Cu + H2SO4 â CuSO4 + H2
quiz.explanation: Charcoal (carbon) reduces copper oxide back to copper.

quiz.q: What is cupellation used for?
quiz.explanation: Cupellation uses lead and bone ash to purify gold.

quiz.q: How can you refine iron in a small forge?
options: A) Heat with iron oxide and hammer
quiz.explanation: Heating iron with iron oxide (hammer scale) and hammering removes carbon.

quiz.q: Why is electrolysis not practical for small-scale aluminium refining?
options: C) It works at room temperature
quiz.explanation: Aluminium electrolysis requires very high current, not available in small workshops.

quiz.q: What flux can be used to refine scrap aluminium?
quiz.explanation: A salt flux of NaCl-KCl helps remove oxides from molten aluminium.

quiz.q: What colour is pure copper?
quiz.explanation: Pure copper has a distinctive salmon pink colour.

quiz.q: Why should refining be done outdoors?
quiz.explanation: Refining produces toxic fumes that must be vented outdoors.

quiz.q: What is the main reducing agent in traditional African iron smelting?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal from local trees was the primary reducing agent.

quiz.q: What temperature is needed to reduce iron oxide with carbon monoxide?
quiz.explanation: Iron oxide reduction with CO works well at around 1200Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the product of roasting copper pyrite (CuFeS2)?
quiz.explanation: Roasting CuFeS2 in air gives copper and iron oxides plus SO2.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding sand as flux in matte smelting?
options: A) To combine with iron oxide to form slag
B) To add silica to the matte
quiz.explanation: Sand (silica) reacts with iron oxide to form a fluid slag.
